title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: The user's holdings transaction log is the authoritative record. For the company, the authoritative record is the audited cash-flow statement — and it tells a different story from the income statement.
epigraph.author: Institutional forensic principle, applied to Netweb FY2019–FY2026 disclosures

web_blocks.html: The purpose of this chapter is to separate accounting profit from economic profit. Netweb's income statement has been spectacular; its cash-flow statement has been intermittent; and its balance sheet has changed character twice in three years. Reading all three together is the only way to judge whether the earnings are real, whether the capital intensity is manageable, and whether the returns on capital genuinely exceed the cost of that capital.

web_blocks.caption: Table 6.1: Audited Profit & Loss and Margin History (FY2019–FY2026, multi-year table)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue compounded at roughly 50% annually for eight years, but operating margin peaked at 16% in FY2023 and has since settled at 13–14% as the mix shifted toward large, lower-margin AI systems deals. Growth is real; margin expansion is not the story — mix and scale are.

web_blocks.caption: Table 6.2: Audited Cash-Flow History and CFO-to-Profit Conversion (FY2019–FY2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Between FY2021 and FY2025 Netweb reported cumulative profits of roughly ₹382 crore while generating cumulative operating cash flow of about ₹27 crore — a conversion ratio under 10%. Only FY2026, with customer advances and faster collections, restored a healthy ₹171 crore of operating cash flow, or about 0.83x net profit. The earnings were never fake, but they were heavily financed.

web_blocks.html: The margin bridge explains the cash story. Netweb's operating margin fell from 16% in FY2023 to 13% in FY2026 for a simple reason: AI systems, now the dominant line, carry a lower gross margin than the bespoke supercomputing projects they replaced in the mix. Management has said repeatedly that a very large deal has an inherently different margin profile from a small one, and that quarterly gross margin is a function of deal mix. What held the operating line at 13–14% despite the mix shift was operating leverage on a near-static overhead base — the same sales, engineering and facilities cost spread over four times the revenue. That is the correct thing to have rewarded, and it is why the EBITDA framework has proven more stable than the gross margin.

The balance sheet has transformed. Equity capital rose from ₹6 crore in FY2019 to ₹12 crore by September 2026, and reserves exploded from ₹5 crore to ₹2,092 crore, reflecting the IPO in 2023, retained earnings, and the ₹1,200 crore QIP in August 2026. Borrowings, which had been run down to near-zero by FY2025, jumped to ₹333 crore at September 2026, and other liabilities — largely payables and customer advances on strategic orders — rose to ₹1,630 crore. On the asset side, fixed assets remain tiny at ₹61 crore, which is the defining feature of an integrator: the capital is not in factories, it is in inventory and receivables.

web_blocks.caption: Table 6.3: Working-Capital and Return Ratios (FY2019–FY2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Debtor days have averaged well over 100, working-capital intensity has swung violently with order timing, and ROCE, while strong at 37% in FY2026, is mechanically flattered by the very low fixed-asset base and will compress as the QIP-funded working capital is deployed. Judge returns on invested capital, not on a flattered ROCE. Note the basis difference versus Chapter 5: these are Screener's ratios, which show FY2026 inventory days of 170 and a cash-conversion cycle of 121, because Screener does not net the customer advances on large strategic orders. Management reports the same year at 84 days by including those advances, and both figures are disclosed here rather than reconciled away.

web_blocks.mechanism: Supermicro built a large, genuine AI-server integration business by being early to GPU-dense server designs and moving faster than the incumbent OEMs. Its revenue exploded with the AI cycle, but because it is an integrator buying the same GPUs and memory as everyone else, its gross and operating margins stayed low and its working capital swelled with inventory. Its share price compounded enormously, then de-rated violently multiple times as the market re-priced the durability and the accounting quality of that growth.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Supermicro's revenue rose from roughly $3.6 billion in FY2022 to about $15 billion in FY2025, yet operating margin stayed in the high single digits to low teens; the stock swung by tens of percent within quarters and drew a short-seller accounting challenge and a delayed filing that erased a large part of its peak market value.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: An integrator riding an AI cycle can grow revenue several-fold while earning thin, cyclical margins, and its valuation will be re-priced the moment growth or accounting quality is questioned. Netweb's 13–15% operating margin is healthy for an integrator, but the business will be judged on cash conversion and order durability, not on the growth headline alone.

web_blocks.html: On returns, the honest framing is that Netweb currently earns a healthy spread over its cost of capital but that the spread will narrow. ROCE was 37.5% and ROE 32.9% in FY2026. Against an estimated cost of equity in the low-to-mid teens for a small-cap Indian systems company, and a weighted average cost of capital somewhere around 12–14%, that is a genuine value-creating spread. But two caveats apply. First, ROCE is flattered by a ₹61 crore fixed-asset base — capital employed here is dominated by working capital, and the numerator (EBIT) benefits from the asset-light model. Second, the QIP has just added ₹1,200 crore of equity to the denominator, so reported ROCE will fall mechanically in FY2027 even if the business improves. Judge the trend in absolute cash returns, not the headline ratio.

web_blocks.title: Dilution, Dividends and the Quality of Capital Allocation
paragraphs: Netweb has funded its growth with a mix of internal accruals, short-term debt and equity. The IPO in 2023 and the ₹1,200 crore QIP in 2026 both added shares, diluting existing holders; promoter holding fell from 75.45% at the time of listing to 64.16% by September 2026, a combination of the IPO, the QIP and small promoter sales. The dividend is token — a 0.07% yield, with a payout that fell to 8% of earnings in FY2026 — which is correct for a company that can reinvest at 30–40% growth.

The deeper question is whether the equity raises were necessary and well-timed. The QIP was priced at ₹4,790 per share in August 2026, near the top of the stock's range, and was explicitly for working capital. Raising equity at a high multiple to fund inventory that supports a ₹2,629 crore order book is defensible capital allocation. The counter-argument — which sceptics make — is that a business this profitable should not need to sell shares to fund routine growth. Both are true: the growth genuinely consumes cash, and the balance sheet is now strong enough to absorb it. The test will be whether the ₹1,200 crore is deployed into orders that earn the guided margin or into inventory that ages.

web_blocks.html: Pulling the forensics together, the earnings quality verdict is nuanced rather than damning. Netweb's profits are real, audited, and backed by genuine revenue; its customers are creditworthy and its receivable days are improving; it is net-debt-negative and earns returns above its cost of capital. What is less clean is the conversion of those profits into cash, which was poor for four of the last eight years and only normalised in FY2026, and the rising inventory that any future slowdown would convert into a write-down risk. This is the profile of a fast-growing, capital-hungry integrator with sound accounting and a genuinely cyclical cash engine — not a fraud, and not a fortress.

book_paragraphs: Profits are an opinion; cash is a fact. That is the maxim you and I must apply to Netweb, because this is a company whose income statement and cash-flow statement have told notably different stories for most of its listed life. Let us follow the cash together, ten years at a time, and see what the numbers really say about the quality of this business.

Begin with the income statement, which is genuinely impressive. Revenue compounded at roughly 50% a year for eight years, from ₹130 crore in FY2019 to ₹2,184 crore in FY2026. Look at Table 6.1 and you will see operating margin rise from 5% to 16% between FY2019 and FY2023, then settle back to 13–14%. That decline is not a deterioration; it is mix. The older business was bespoke supercomputing with premium margins; the newer business is large AI systems with lower ones. What saved the operating line was leverage on overheads — the same cost base carrying four times the revenue.

Now turn to the cash-flow statement, in Table 6.2, and watch the mood change. From FY2021 to FY2025, Netweb reported cumulative profits of roughly ₹382 crore but generated cumulative operating cash flow of about ₹27 crore. Read that sentence again. For four years, this company earned profits on paper and barely converted them into cash, because every new order required buying GPUs and memory before the customer paid. Only in FY2026 did operating cash flow of ₹171 crore finally restore a healthy relationship with net profit of ₹206 crore — a conversion ratio of about 0.83x. The profits were never fabricated. But they were, for years, financed by the balance sheet rather than delivered as cash.

The balance sheet tells you where the money went, and it is not the factory. Fixed assets are a mere ₹61 crore — almost nothing. The capital is in inventory and receivables. Borrowings, which had been paid down to near-zero by FY2025, climbed back to ₹333 crore by September 2026, and other liabilities reached ₹1,630 crore, largely payables and customer advances on large orders. Equity capital rose from ₹6 crore to ₹12 crore and reserves from ₹5 crore to ₹2,092 crore, transformed by the 2023 IPO and the 2026 QIP. This is the balance sheet of an asset-light integrator: no heavy plants, but a working-capital engine that must be continuously fed.

Consider Supermicro, the cautionary parallel, because it is the closest listed analogue to what Netweb does. Supermicro grew revenue from about $3.6 billion in FY2022 to roughly $15 billion by FY2025 on the same AI-server cycle Netweb is riding — genuine, enormous growth. But its operating margins stayed thin, its working capital swelled with inventory, and its share price has de-rated violently several times, including a short-seller accounting challenge and a delayed filing that wiped out a large part of its peak value. The lesson is not that growth is bad; it is that the market will not pay a premium forever for an integrator whose margins are thin and whose cash conversion is uncertain. The moment growth wobbles or accounting quality is questioned, the multiple compresses fast.

So what is the honest earnings-quality verdict? Look at the returns. ROCE was 37.5% and ROE 32.9% in FY2026 — comfortably above any reasonable estimate of Netweb's cost of capital, somewhere around 12–14%. That is genuine value creation, and it is the strongest part of the forensic picture. But be careful with the ratio: it is flattered by the tiny fixed-asset base, and it will fall mechanically in FY2027 because the ₹1,200 crore QIP has just enlarged the equity denominator. Judge whether the incremental capital earns its keep, not whether the headline ROCE is pretty.

One more judgement call, on dilution. Promoter holding has fallen from 75.45% at listing to 64.16% by September 2026 — partly the IPO, partly the QIP, partly small promoter sales. The dividend is token, at an 8% payout and a 0.07% yield, which is the right choice for a company that can reinvest at 30–40%. But the QIP raises the question the sceptics keep asking: why does a business this profitable need to sell shares to fund its own growth? The answer is that growth, not profit, consumes the cash — and buying components for a ₹2,629 crore order book is the definition of cash-hungry growth.

There is one more forensic habit worth building, and it is the one that catches most integrators before the market does: reconcile the income statement to the balance sheet every quarter, not once a year. When revenue rises, ask where the corresponding asset went. In Netweb's case the answer is almost always inventory or receivables, and the useful test is whether those two are growing faster than revenue. In FY2026 receivables actually improved while inventory rose sharply, which the company attributes to deliberate pre-positioning against component lead times. That explanation is credible in a supply-constrained GPU market, but it is also exactly the explanation every integrator gives before an inventory write-down. The discipline is not to disbelieve management; it is to track the ratio and to treat a sustained rise in inventory days without a matching rise in the order book as the earliest available warning that the cycle has turned.

Bring the threads together, and the verdict on financial quality is nuanced rather than damning. Netweb's profits are real and audited; its customers are creditworthy; its receivable days are improving; it is net-debt-negative and earns above its cost of capital. What is less clean is the long history of poor cash conversion and the rising inventory that any slowdown would turn into a write-down risk. This is the profile of a fast-growing, capital-hungry, soundly-accounted integrator with a genuinely cyclical cash engine — not a fraud, and not a fortress. Price it accordingly.

book_callouts.title: The Four-Year Cash Gap
book_callouts.text: The single most important line in this chapter is the cumulative gap between profit and operating cash flow from FY2021 to FY2025: about ₹382 crore of profit against about ₹27 crore of cash. That gap is the reason the company needed the QIP, and it is the reason you should treat every future 'record profit' headline with the question: how much of it arrived as cash? The gap has closed for now. Watching whether it stays closed is the core of holding this stock.
